framing_assertion.rationale: The initial request (chatbot to stop customers waiting for refund answers) from SH-SUP, whose noted bias is to frame everything as response speed, asserts the backlog's root cause is a missing automated answer channel.

hypotheses.statement: Customers wait because there is no automated channel to get refund status answers; a chatbot answering faster would resolve the backlog.
hypotheses.rationale: This is SH-SUP's stated framing and the premise behind the chatbot request; SH-SUP's bias toward framing issues as response speed means this needs independent verification rather than acceptance.

hypotheses.statement: Many tickets are status-check follow-ups generated because actual refund payments are delayed in processing, not because customers lack a way to ask.
hypotheses.rationale: If refunds themselves are slow (DA-PAY), a chatbot would only automate delivery of 'still pending' answers without fixing the underlying delay, requiring a payment-process fix instead.
discriminating_evidence: correlation between ticket creation timestamps and refund payment status in DA-PAY

hypotheses.statement: The backlog stems from an unusually high volume of refund tickets (e.g., policy confusion or a triggering event), overwhelming support regardless of response automation.
hypotheses.rationale: High inbound volume with normal per-ticket response times would point to a demand-side cause (policy clarity, defect) rather than a communication-channel gap, changing the recommended fix.
discriminating_evidence: ticket-db ticket volume trend over time
ticket-db categorization of refund ticket reasons

hypotheses.statement: Delays originate in the refund process (P-REF) itself, e.g., slow or broken handoffs between support and payment teams, which produces slow answers independent of the answering channel.
hypotheses.rationale: If the bottleneck is internal process handoffs rather than customer-facing communication, the fix is process redesign, not a customer-facing chatbot.

output.summary: The support lead (SH-SUP) initially asked for a chatbot so customers "stop waiting for answers about refunds" (CL-01, CL-02, E-03), framing the backlog as a missing automated response channel. Investigation evidence contradicted that framing: all 5 sampled payment-db refund_failures records show status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), and ticket-db shows median response time of 2.0h against a 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-02), meaning answer speed is not the bottleneck. The problem definition (PD-1) was reset to: refund-related tickets accumulate because refunds themselves fail at payment processing due to malformed IBAN data, generating status-check follow-ups, not because customers lack a channel to ask. The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two critical unknowns (ticket root-cause mix, bank-api availability for reprocessing) as verification obligations (VOBs) rather than blocking the whole effort. The released scope was limited to diagnosing the IBAN validation defect in DA-PAY (work item W-WI-01, DONE); correcting malformed IBANs and reprocessing refunds through bank-api was explicitly left unfinished. The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with no holds: the diagnosis work was completed and is being released, while the parts of the original scope that are blocked (reprocessing) or unresolved (full-population confirmation, ticket-to-IBAN linkage) are carried forward as documented limitations rather than preventing release of what was finished.
key_points: Original stakeholder request was for a chatbot to speed up answers (CL-01/CL-02/E-03), but E-01 (5/5 sampled refund failures = FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT) and E-02 (median 2.0h response vs 24h SLA over 900 tickets) contradicted that framing, leading to H-COMM-CHANNEL-GAP being REJECTED and H-IBAN-FORMAT-DEFECT / H-REFUND-PROCESSING-DELAY being SUPPORTED.

The problem was redefined (PD-1) as refunds failing in payment-db due to malformed IBAN data, which generates status-check tickets, distinct from and not explained by slow answering (evidence_refs E-01, E-02).

The DEFINE gate result was CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two HIGH-criticality unknowns -- U-TICKET-ROOT-CAUSE-MIX and U-BANK-API-AVAILABILITY-FOR-RE -- as VOBs rather than resolving them before proceeding.

The released scope (solution_design SD-1) was narrowed to 'diagnose_iban_validation_defect:DA-PAY', completed as work item W-WI-01 (status DONE); correcting IBANs and reprocessing refunds (SR-CORRECT-AND-REPROCESS-REFUND) was marked not feasible in contest time and left unfinished.

The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with an empty hold list, meaning the completed diagnosis is released while unresolved items are documented as limitations rather than blocking release.

Both open VOBs (VOB-U-TICKET-ROOT-CAUSE-MIX, VOB-U-BANK-API-AVAILABILITY-FOR-RE) have blocking_scope that falls outside the actual release scope, which is why they did not force a hold on this release.
limitations_explained: The DEFINE gate only reached CONDITIONAL_PASS; two critical unknowns were deferred to VOBs rather than resolved, per the define_gate_result event.

VOB-U-TICKET-ROOT-CAUSE-MIX is still open: it is unknown what share of the 900 tickets are actually refund-status follow-ups tied to IBAN failures versus other causes (U-TICKET-ROOT-CAUSE-MIX), but its blocking_scope (classify_ticket_root_causes:DA-TCK) is outside this release's scope.

VOB-U-BANK-API-AVAILABILITY-FOR-RE is still open: whether refund reprocessing can even be executed is unresolved because bank-api is DEGRADED (ACCESS_DENIED/NOT_TRANSIENT hold, no fallback), but its blocking_scope (reprocess_failed_refunds:DA-PAY) is outside this release.
The bank-api tool is currently DEGRADED (runtime.tool_health), which independently blocks any correction/reprocessing of refunds regardless of how good the diagnosis is.
Correcting malformed IBAN values on existing failed refund records and reprocessing them through bank-api remains unfinished work (solution_design.unfinished_scope).

The root-cause evidence (E-01) rests on only 5 sampled refund_failures records; DA-PAY's completeness is UNKNOWN (assumption A-SAMPLE-REPRESENTATIVE), so it is not established whether this sample represents the full failure population.

The link between support tickets and IBAN-related refund failures is an assumption (A-TICKETS-LINKED-TO-IBAN-FAILU), not directly evidenced by ticket content -- no ticket-level data was cited confirming this connection.
